title: Why You Shouldn't Shush Your Students; And What To Do Instead
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin treats shushing as a visible symptom of struggling classroom management, arguing it grows less effective the more it's used and chips away at a teacher's likeability and authority. In its place he offers an eight-step system: decide the desired voice level before an activity begins, model it precisely, have students practice it, observe closely once the activity starts, stop the activity (rather than shush) if noise exceeds expectations, remind students of the expectation and the consequence for exceeding it, enforce that consequence when needed, and eventually standardize a numbered scale of voice levels (from silence to whole-class sharing) posted for reference. He notes group discussions naturally get louder and should be redirected with a pause rather than a consequence. The piece closes by claiming the method works at any grade level once students get used to it.
points: Shushing loses effectiveness the more it's used and signals shaky classroom management to students.
Decide and model the exact voice level you want before an activity begins—don't assume students already know.
Stop the activity and signal for attention instead of shushing when noise exceeds the expectation.
Standardize a numbered voice-level scale (e.g., Level 0 to Level 3) and post it for quick reference.
For natural loudness in group discussions, pause and reset with deep breaths rather than issuing a consequence.
quotes: Shushing students to quiet them down is associated with shaky-at-best classroom management, chronically distracted students, and a mountain of stress.

Before starting any activity, decide the voice level you want from your students. It’s important you consider this ahead of time. After all, if you don’t know what you want, your students won’t know either.
If at any time their voice level gets louder than your expectation, instead of shushing your students, stop the activity by signaling for their attention.

Setting voice level expectations—for partner sharing, group work, browsing in the library, or just a walk across campus—through the super-effective one-two combination of detailed modeling and student practice works at any grade level.
Behind tight shoulders, tired eyes, and index finger poised over puckered lips, you’ll find a teacher struggling to keep his or her head above water.
And because it becomes progressively less effective the more you do it, shushing promises more and more frustration as the school year rolls on.
